========================================================
Empirical Research Plan
========================================================

--------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences with Continuous Treatment Intensity (often called “shift-share” or “dose-response” DiD) supplemented by an event-study specification.

Rationale  
• Medicare arrived everywhere at the same moment (July 1966), but the size of the insurance shock differed systematically with each state’s pre-1965 share of uninsured elderly.  
• Because the pre-Medicare uninsurance rate is predetermined (measured in 1963) and sharply predicts the coverage gain, interacting it with a post-1966 dummy captures exogenous variation in the *dose* of the Medicare shock.  
• The panel (1948-1975) allows us to compare spending trends in high- versus low-shock states before and after the policy, controlling for state and year fixed effects.  
• An event-study version (year dummies interacted with pre-uninsurance) can visually test parallel trends and time-path dynamics.

--------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
TREAT_s ≡ pre-Medicare uninsurance rate among 65+ in state s (one number per state, measured in 1963; higher = bigger shock).

Treatment timing  
POST_t = 1 for 1966–1975 (0 for 1948–1965). The first exposed year is 1966; robustness will drop 1966 (“phase-in”) in sensitivity checks.

Continuous DiD specification  
Outcome_s,t = α + β (TREAT_s × POST_t) + γ_s + δ_t + X_s,t θ + ε_s,t

• β is the causal effect of a unit (1 ppt) difference in the coverage shock on total hospital spending per capita.

Counterfactual / control  
States with low pre-uninsurance (CT, MN, etc.) serve as comparison units for states with high uninsurance (MS, AL). All states are observed both pre and post; the identifying variation is the differential change correlated with TREAT_s.

--------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends (Conditional)  
Absent Medicare, total hospital spending in high- and low-uninsurance states would have evolved in parallel. Plausibility: 1948-1965 saw no nationwide elderly-specific insurance expansions; pre-period data allow graphical and statistical tests.

A2. No Simultaneous Confounders Correlated with TREAT_s  
No other 1960s policy generated spending shocks whose intensity is mechanically tied to the 1963 elderly uninsurance rate. Plausibility: Medicaid began in 1966 but eligibility for the elderly was not linked to pre-uninsurance; we will control for Medicaid take-up and state policy dummies.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Cross-State Spillovers)  
Hospital capacity expansions in high-shock states do not crowd out or flood neighboring states in a way that biases state-level spending. Cross-state care for the elderly was rare in the 1960s; we will show results are similar when bordering states are grouped or when using regional clusters.

A4. Exogeneity of Pre-Uninsurance  
The 1963 elderly uninsurance share is predetermined and unaffected by post-1966 outcomes; measurement error is classical. The 1963 National Health Survey preceded the policy debate, supporting exogeneity.

--------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential Pre-Trends  
• Test visually with event study (β_t for t ≤ 1965).  
• Include state-specific linear time trends.  
• Placebo policy year (pretend Medicare started in 1961) to check for spurious breaks.

T2. Concurrent Medicaid or War-on-Poverty Programs  
• Control for Medicaid spending per capita interacted with eligibility rules.  
• Re-estimate excluding AFDC/poverty controls; show β stable.  
• Instrument TREAT_s × POST_t with (1 – pre-coverage) × POST_t; same numerically but demonstrates theoretical first-stage.

T3. Differential Migration of Elderly  
• Use Census IPUMS to show net interstate migration of 65+ is <1% during 1960-70 and uncorrelated with 1963 coverage.  
• Repeat regressions with hospital spending per *resident* adjusted by population denominator that excludes migrants (using Census year stocks).

--------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)
library(fixest)     # fast fixed-effects
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data
aha <- fread("AHA_state_year_1948_1975.csv")  # contains spend, beds, etc.
ins <- fread("elderly_uninsurance_1963.csv")  # one row per state: uninsured63

# 2. Merge and construct variables
dt <- merge(aha, ins, by = "state")
dt[, post := (year >= 1966)]
dt[, treat := uninsured63]                   # continuous "dose"
dt[, treat_post := treat * post]

# Control variables (already in dt): income_pc, urban_share, physicians_pc, etc.
# Log outcome
dt[, ln_spend_pc := log(total_spending_pc)]

# 3. Main DiD regression
did_mod <- feols(ln_spend_pc ~ treat_post + income_pc + urban_share +
                 physicians_pc | state + year,
                 cluster = ~state,
                 data = dt)
summary(did_mod)

# 4. Event-study
dt[, rel_year := year - 1966]
evt_mod <- feols(ln_spend_pc ~ i(rel_year, treat, ref = -1) +
                 income_pc + urban_share + physicians_pc |
                 state + year,
                 cluster = ~state,
                 data = dt[rel_year >= -10 & rel_year <= 9])
iplot(evt_mod, xlab = "Years relative to 1966", main = "Event-study: Medicare shock")

# 5. Robustness: add state linear trends
did_trend <- feols(ln_spend_pc ~ treat_post + income_pc + urban_share +
                   physicians_pc | state + year[state] ,
                   cluster = ~state,
                   data = dt)
summary(did_trend)

# 6. Save results
etable(list(Main = did_mod, Trend = did_trend), file = "results.tex")
```

--------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------
Theory: Newly insured elderly raise demand for inpatient care. Hospitals respond by expanding capacity (beds, staff) that also serves non-elderly patients, pushing up *total* spending.

Direction: β > 0.

Magnitude (back-of-envelope): If a 40 ppt increase in coverage (e.g., MS) raises total hospital spending per capita by, say, 12%, that implies β ≈ 0.30 log-points per 100 ppt, or 0.003 per 1 ppt. We therefore expect β ≈ 0.25–0.35 (elasticity 0.25–0.35).

--------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------
C1: Parallel pre-trends visually satisfied      → 1  
C2: No policy anticipation before 1965          → 1  
C3: No differential contemporaneous shocks      → 0.5 (Medicaid risk)  
C4: Stable unit composition/no migration bias   → 0.5  
C5: Correct specification & standard errors     → 1  

Total = 4 / 5 – credible but vigilance required.

========================================================
